title: CompBio and MIRaS-a multi-omic analysis platform built on a memory-based intelligence engine.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unpacked the Europe PMC supplement zip (6.33 MB) and opened the inner SupplementaryMaterial_CompBio_MIRAS2026.xlsx: 40 sheets, every one a small benchmark-output table (largest 2,507 rows = one GSEA run; most 50-400 rows), with multi-row titles and cells holding text blobs like 'Name=...Score=164769.45', 'Coordinates=X: -0.63,Y: -0.93,Z: 1.36'. Read the Index sheet listing all 27 supplementary tables. Queried the Zenodo API for record 18602034/18602035: metadata returns but the file list is empty and https://zenodo.org/api/records/18602035/files returns HTTP 403 FORBIDDEN; the landing page contains 'Embargo', 'restricted' and 'Request access', so miras.zip and compbio.zip are not downloadable. Grepped the open-access full text for methods, data availability and access terms.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the Generalized Memory Model (GeMM, the engine's stored-knowledge index) version 2.9 was built from the Q1 2025 PubMed release with 38,355,642 abstracts and 6,600,121 full-text articles; that the platform is 'freely available to all academic and non-profit institutions'; the experimental provenance of the benchmark gene lists (Mootha, Brass, VanDussen, Tsingas, Malique & Sun, Silver, Malecki, LOPAC1280 compound screen). I did not create a platform account or run the tool.

a1_downloadable.note: The only freely downloadable artifact is the supplementary Excel/PDF of benchmark outputs, which I opened. The actual software (miras.zip, compbio.zip) on Zenodo is embargoed: the files API returns HTTP 403 and the page says 'Request access'. The GeMM knowledge index itself is never distributed, and using the platform requires an academic account.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no prediction target anywhere in the files. The sheets hold enrichment outputs (theme names, scores, P-values, 3-D map coordinates) for roughly a dozen hand-picked gene lists; any machine-learning label would have to be invented and constructed from scratch across sheets with inconsistent headers.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs would be gene lists, which are present only as bare gene symbols in three narrow sheets (STable6: 1,058 rows across 3 lists; STable15: 721 rows across 3 lists). No expression values, no sequences, no per-gene features of any kind accompany them.

a4_units_stated.note: The score columns ('Score=164769.45', 'NESCore', 'Theme Pvalue') are platform-internal quantities on an undocumented scale; no units are given and the normalized enrichment score is not comparable across tools.

a5_enough_rows.note: Counted in the file: the biggest sheet is 2,507 rows but that is one GSEA result list for one experiment. The real unit of analysis is the gene list or the benchmark comparison, and there are about 10 gene lists and 50 Hallmark gene sets — two orders of magnitude under the ~1,500-row bar.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-sized; this is the only Part A check that passes cleanly. The engine behind it, however, indexes 45 million documents and is explicitly described as resource-heavy.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: What I could cross-check lines up: 50 MSigDB Hallmark gene sets in STable1 (57 rows with headers), and the per-tool pathway and gene-mapping counts in STable7 match the text's benchmarking narrative.

a8_label_provenance.note: Fatal and unambiguous. Every quantitative value in the supplement is the output of a software tool — CompBio/MIRaS itself, or the comparators GSEA, Metascape, ToppGene and GeneAgent. Training on these would distil another tool's scores, with that tool's accuracy as the ceiling and no physical measurement anywhere underneath.

existing_models.name: CompBio / MIRaS (this paper) — a literature-memory reasoning engine that names biological themes for a gene list
existing_models.score_and_split: Reports recovering 49 or 50 of the 50 MSigDB Hallmark gene sets from their own member genes (STable1), plus tolerance to progressive gene-list noise; no held-out split, since the engine is not trained.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: They frame curated-pathway dependence and large language model hallucination as the problems solved, and do not name a clear open problem; the engine's reliance on what the literature happens to contain is the implicit gap.

existing_models.name: GeneAgent (Nature Methods 2025) — a GPT-4 based agent that names gene-set functions and checks its own claims against biological databases
existing_models.score_and_split: Evaluated on 1,106 gene sets from several sources; reported as consistently more accurate than plain GPT-4, with 92% of its self-verification decisions judged correct. Code is on GitHub (ncbi-nlp/GeneAgent) but it needs a commercial GPT-4 key.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Hallucination in gene-set naming, and verification of claims that no database covers.

existing_models.name: GSEA, Metascape, ToppGene, Enrichr — the standard open gene-set enrichment tools, all used as comparators in this paper
existing_models.score_and_split: Decades of published benchmarks; no single number applies. All are freely installable and were run by the authors on the same gene lists.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Dependence on human-curated pathway databases, and poor coverage of biology outside those databases.

integration.partner_dataset: none — the supplement carries only gene symbols and tool-generated theme names, no standard identifiers to join on
integration.join_key: gene symbol (unversioned, human and mouse mixed across sheets)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written: the files contain one tool's opinions about a dozen gene lists, so a join would add context to outputs rather than to measurements.

controls.positive_control: The paper does supply one — recovery of the 50 MSigDB Hallmark gene sets from their member genes — but it controls their tool, not any model we would build.
controls.negative_control: Their signal-reduction experiment (replacing Hallmark genes with random genes, 0-100%) is a genuine negative control, again for their tool.
controls.external_validation: None available to us: the engine, its knowledge index and its scoring are not distributed, so no result of theirs can be reproduced or extended.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible. There is no measured outcome in these files, so any model trained on them would be predicting what CompBio, GSEA or ToppGene said about ten gene lists.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a list of genes to predict which biological themes an enrichment tool would report for it.
plain_idea.train_on: The only candidate inputs are bare gene symbols from about ten benchmark gene lists (1,058 symbols in one sheet, 721 in another) plus the 50 MSigDB Hallmark gene sets; no expression values or sequences accompany them.
plain_idea.predict: The theme names, enrichment scores and P-values that the CompBio platform or a comparator tool emitted. The 'true answer' is software output, not a measurement made in a lab.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: It would not be worthwhile: the best possible result is reproducing an existing tool from a few dozen of its own outputs. The only thing learned here is that software-platform papers with embargoed code are dead ends for modelling.

more_or_better_data.why: GeneAgent was evaluated on 1,106 gene sets and the classical tools on hundreds of benchmark datasets; this supplement offers roughly ten gene lists and 50 Hallmark sets. We would have two orders of magnitude less data than the existing work.

confidence_score.why: No replicates and no repeated measurements of anything — each sheet is a single run of a single tool on a single gene list, so per-prediction uncertainty cannot be estimated. The paper's own P-values already serve that role for their engine.

models_beatable.why: The direct competitor, GeneAgent (2025), is a GPT-4 agent with public code evaluated on 1,106 gene sets, and GSEA/Metascape/ToppGene are mature, freely installable and universally used. Nothing in these files supports beating any of them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on every condition: the paper's own engine cannot be run as a baseline because it is embargoed, there is no measured quantity for new data to join to, and no evaluation split exists.

ml_idea: None viable. The paper describes a literature-memory reasoning engine for interpreting omics gene lists; its supplement is a 40-sheet benchmarking report, not a dataset. The nearest conceivable project — learning to reproduce the engine's theme assignments from gene lists — fails A8 by construction (the label is another tool's output) and A5 by a wide margin (about ten gene lists).

effort.compute_note: Measured the unpacked supplement at ~14 MB and opened the 40-sheet workbook in read-only mode in seconds. No modelling estimates apply because there is no feature/label table to build.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Ask what physical measurement any number in the supplement traces back to. The answer is none — every value is a tool's enrichment score — and that check takes five minutes with the Index sheet.

verdict_reason: A software-platform paper, not a dataset. Verified in the files: the supplement is 40 sheets of benchmarking output (largest 2,507 rows, and that is one GSEA run for one experiment), where every quantitative value is produced by CompBio, GSEA, Metascape, ToppGene or GeneAgent rather than measured — an outright A8 failure, since any model would distil another tool. A2 fails too (no target column exists; one would have to be invented), and A5 fails because the real unit is the gene list and there are about ten. A1 fails as well: the Zenodo code deposit is embargoed (files API returns HTTP 403, landing page says 'Request access'), the 45-million-document knowledge index is never distributed, and the platform itself needs an academic account. The field is also well served by open tools and by GeneAgent (2025, 1,106 gene sets).
